title: Reranking
shortDefinition: A two-stage retrieval technique that reorders initially retrieved documents by relevance before passing them to an LLM.
definition: Reranking is a two-stage retrieval technique for RAG systems where an initial fast retrieval step (using vector similarity) fetches a broader set of candidate documents, and a second, more computationally expensive reranker model then reorders those candidates by a more precise relevance estimate before the top results are passed to the LLM for answer generation. Reranking frequently delivers significant RAG quality improvements because the initial vector similarity retrieval, while fast, doesn't always surface the most relevant documents at the top — reranking applies a more nuanced relevance model to the subset of candidates already retrieved.

sections.title: Why initial vector retrieval isn't always enough
sections.description: Vector similarity search is fast but can't always capture nuanced relevance distinctions.

content.text: Vector similarity search retrieves documents whose embeddings are mathematically close to the query's embedding — fast and effective for semantic matching, but using a single embedding vector per document and query that can't always capture nuanced relevance distinctions. A reranker model (typically a cross-encoder) jointly encodes the query and each candidate document together, allowing much more nuanced relevance assessment than comparing separately-encoded embeddings — at significantly higher computational cost, which is why it's applied only to the smaller set of already-retrieved candidates rather than the entire document corpus.

items: Vector retrieval — fast but limited to single-embedding comparisons.
Reranker — cross-encoder considers query and document together.
Nuanced relevance — better assessment of true relevance.
Computational cost — higher, applied only to candidate subset.
Complementary — reranking fixes what vector retrieval misses.

content.title: The key insight
content.text: Vector retrieval is fast but imperfect — reranking applies a more nuanced model to a small set of candidates, fixing ordering issues.

sections.title: Bi-encoders vs. cross-encoders: the architecture behind reranking
sections.description: Bi-encoders power fast initial retrieval; cross-encoders power accurate reranking.

content.text: Initial vector retrieval uses bi-encoders — the query and each document are encoded independently into comparable embedding vectors, which is fast because document embeddings can be pre-computed and stored. Rerankers typically use cross-encoders — the query and each candidate document are encoded together, allowing the model to consider their full interaction, which produces more accurate relevance scores but can't be pre-computed (it requires real-time computation for every query-document pair). This is exactly why reranking is a second-stage filter: you can't cross-encode every document in a large corpus for every query, but you can cross-encode the small set of already-retrieved candidates.

content.title: The two-stage tradeoff
content.text: Bi-encoders are fast enough for entire corpus retrieval. Cross-encoders are accurate enough for reranking a small candidate set. Together, they balance speed and quality.

items: "Our RAG system already uses good embeddings — do we also need reranking?" — Often yes, if retrieved document ordering is a limiting factor — the best embedding models still produce imperfect ranking for nuanced queries, and a well-implemented reranker frequently delivers meaningful answer quality improvements even starting from strong initial retrieval.

"How much will this cost?" — $20,000–$90,000 depending on whether this is adding reranking to an existing pipeline or part of a broader RAG quality optimization engagement. Fixed quote after Discovery.

"Will reranking make our RAG system significantly slower?" — Reranking adds latency since it requires additional model inference on retrieved candidates; ClickMasters designs reranking to minimize latency impact — batching candidate scoring, caching where possible, and validating acceptable response time after implementation.
"Does reranking replace or complement vector similarity retrieval?" — Complement — vector retrieval first fetches candidates quickly; reranking then reorders those candidates more precisely.

content.text: Reranking has limitations. It adds latency and computational cost. Cross-encoder models are more expensive to run than vector similarity search. Reranking can amplify errors if the initial retrieval fails to include relevant documents. Performance depends on the quality of the reranker model. It requires careful tuning to balance quality and latency, and may not significantly improve quality if initial retrieval is already very strong. Reranking can also be more complex to implement and maintain than single-stage retrieval.

items: Latency overhead — adds additional model inference.

Tuning required — balance quality and latency.

content.title: Important
content.text: Reranking is a quality improvement technique with a cost tradeoff. Validate that the quality gain justifies the added latency and cost for your specific use case.

Implementing reranking effectively requires careful model selection, latency optimization, and quality validation. The following practices can help ensure reranking delivers quality gains without excessive latency cost.

content.title: Key metric
content.text: Measure recall improvement at top-k — does reranking improve the quality of documents that reach the LLM? This is the metric that matters for answer quality.

items.question: How much does reranking typically improve RAG answer quality?
items.answer: This varies by use case and initial retrieval quality; ClickMasters measures actual improvement via retrieval quality metrics for your specific system rather than citing a generic percentage.

items.question: Does reranking replace or complement vector similarity retrieval?
items.answer: Complement — vector retrieval first fetches candidates quickly; reranking then reorders those candidates more precisely. They work sequentially, not as alternatives.

items.answer: A poorly configured reranker can reorder candidates suboptimally; ClickMasters validates quality improvement with retrieval metrics before committing reranking to production.

items.answer: 6–16 weeks depending on whether it's reranking alone or part of a broader RAG quality optimization engagement.

items.question: Is reranking relevant for semantic search outside of RAG?
items.answer: Yes, the same two-stage retrieval-then-rerank pattern improves standalone semantic search quality, not only RAG pipelines.

items.question: What is the difference between bi-encoders and cross-encoders?
items.answer: Bi-encoders encode query and documents separately, enabling fast retrieval from large corpora. Cross-encoders encode them together, providing more accurate relevance scores but requiring computation per query-document pair.

items.question: How many candidates should be retrieved before reranking?
items.answer: Typically 50-200 candidates are retrieved initially, then reranked to return the top 5-10. The right number depends on your quality/latency tradeoff. ClickMasters optimizes this for your use case.

items.question: Can reranking be combined with hybrid search?
items.answer: Yes — hybrid search (vector + keyword) can be used for initial retrieval, followed by reranking for precise ordering. This combines the strengths of all three approaches.

items.question: What is the relationship between reranking and retrieval quality metrics?
items.answer: Reranking improves retrieval quality metrics like precision@k and recall@k. Measuring these metrics before and after reranking validates that it's actually improving retrieval quality.
